video_title: Lindy Teammate: Flo Crivello on Multiplayer Agents, Memory & Why He'd Ban the Chinese Models He Uses
gist: Flo Crivello, founder/CEO of Lindy, launches Lindy Teammate — a Slack-resident multiplayer AI employee that crawls a company's entire Slack/Notion/meeting history into a git-backed, agent-maintained memory file system — and discloses unusually specific engineering and unit economics: an 85% cache rate, negative gross margins on the new product, DeepSeek as the default main-driver model, an 8x error-rate drop from a self-improvement loop, and ~$10k of automated prompt re-optimization per new frontier model release. He argues context now matters more than intelligence, that RAG loses to agent-managed file-system memory, that division of labor is a bad reason to build multi-agent systems, and that we are in a temporary 'centaur' phase before humans become noise. He closes with the contrarian position that Chinese frontier models — including the DeepSeek his own company runs on — should be banned in the US, while conceding an insurance/audit regime as a possible compromise.

themes.theme: Multiplayer AI employees as the next product form factor

insights.claim: Lindy's new product, Lindy Teammate, is an AI employee that lives inside a company's Slack, connects to its tools, and accumulates shared team context rather than per-user context — Crivello frames this multiplayer shift as the analog of moving from emailed document revisions to Google Docs.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Single-player chat assistants may be a transitional form factor; incumbents whose agents lack shared org memory and a collaboration-surface home are exposed to Slack-native multiplayer entrants.
insights.quote: I compare the difference between multiplayer and single player AI as between like sending each other weird documents and Google Docs like an actual shared document.

insights.claim: Crivello argues that as AGI arrives, raw intelligence matters less and context matters more, illustrating with the claim that John von Neumann magically appearing at your office would be less useful over the next hour than a random coworker who has the context.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Defensibility in the agent layer is shifting from model access to accumulated proprietary org context — a durable moat argument for context-hoarding application companies over thin model wrappers.
insights.quote: as we now arguably have AGI, intelligence actually matters less and less comparatively speaking and context matters more and more

insights.claim: Crivello claims agents are already better than humans at onboarding, because most human onboarding leans on wikis and written documentation that is out of date the moment it is written, whereas agents can ingest the messy live Slack record directly.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: If agent onboarding beats human onboarding, the cost of adding an AI 'headcount' collapses toward zero marginal ramp time — a key input to the drop-in-knowledge-worker substitution thesis.
insights.quote: as everyone knows, the moment written documentation is written, it's out of date

insights.claim: Lindy treats meetings as a first-class citizen in its memory system rather than relying on external notetakers, on the view that roughly 90% of the most up-to-date company knowledge lives in meetings and everything that matters has a meeting around it.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Standalone meeting-recording tools like Granola risk being commoditized as a feature inside memory-owning agent platforms; watch for consolidation pressure on that category.
insights.quote: I think like those multiplayer agentic systems cannot really get meetings to like granola or whatever like I think you have to really incorporate it in your system as a first class citizen

insights.claim: Lindy has been forced to solve the privacy problem of multiplayer memory with a two-tier design — a public workspace layer and a private personal layer — populated by a background 'memory agent' that Crivello says runs roughly every 15 minutes rather than on a daily sleep cycle.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: The public/private tiering is the practical gating factor for enterprise adoption of org-wide agent memory; vendors without a credible answer will stall in security review.
insights.quote: We call it napping not sleeping. So like it runs every something like 15 minutes like why why would you need to sleep every 24 hours?

insights.claim: Rather than building complex permission structures for sensitive historical data, Lindy lets each user edit a plain-text meta-memory prompt (memory.md) that is injected into the memory agent's context window at all times, with instructions like what never to remember or which folders never to surface.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Prompt-level governance instead of schema-level permissioning is cheap to ship but is an audit and liability surface enterprises may not accept — a differentiator to probe in diligence.
insights.quote: your memory agent has that memory prompt injected in its context window at every moment

insights.claim: Crivello says organizations are rewriting the social contract around historical data in real time, because people who shared things in private Slack messages or calls never expected that content to land in a central agent repository accessible to colleagues.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz and Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Retroactive ingestion of years of internal communications is a live legal and cultural risk that could generate the first big enterprise-agent backlash or regulation.

insights.claim: Crivello predicts the next six months of AI product development will be dominated by multiplayer AI and human-AI hybrid 'Iron Man suit' products rather than single-user assistants.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A near-dated, falsifiable roadmap call for the agent application layer — useful for timing bets on collaboration-surface-native agent startups.
insights.quote: I do believe the next six months are going to be about multiplayer AI and about this like Iron Man suit

insights.claim: Crivello is explicitly bearish on RAG as the primary memory approach and bullish on agent-managed text-and-file-system memory, because an agent with its own meta-memory understands what it is looking at and the memory stays inspectable and editable.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A direct negative signal for pure vector-DB/RAG-infrastructure businesses and a positive one for agent-native file-system and memory-orchestration vendors.
insights.quote: I think this is why I'm ultimately quite bearish on rag as an approach and I'm very bullish on on on this like agentic management approach because you have an actual agent which has its own memory

insights.claim: Lindy's memory agent exhibited emergent curation behavior: on first crawling a customer's Slack it learns to identify and permanently ignore automated log channels, rather than needing hand-coded heuristics for each idiosyncratic data source.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: If curation emerges rather than being engineered, the cost of onboarding messy enterprise data drops sharply — undercutting data-cleaning and connector-heavy middleware.
insights.quote: the first time the memory agent crawls the Slack, it finds some of those channels like many organizations have them like those like log channels and it learns to ignore them

insights.claim: Crivello compares memory poisoning to training-data poisoning: a single false memory gets drowned out by the correct data if the system holds enough memories and actually understands them, which is why he trusts agentic curation over hand-tuned heuristics.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Implies scale of ingested context is itself a robustness property — favoring vendors who ingest everything over those who curate narrowly.

insights.claim: Lindy routes all memory access through a single memory agent even though other agents could read the file system directly, so that it can log every query, answer and hop count, then have the agent restructure its own memory during 'napping' to minimize hops for frequently asked questions.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Query logs turn memory into a self-optimizing cache — a compounding advantage that accrues with usage and is hard for a new entrant to replicate cold.
insights.quote: it will it restructure its own memory to reduce the number of hops that is needed to retrieve like the most frequently asked questions

insights.claim: Lindy still uses some RAG, implemented as bidirectional hypothesis-driven retrieval: searching over generated candidate answers rather than the question, and attaching auto-generated questions to found answers, because a hypothesis is semantically closer to the answer than the question is.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A concrete, cheap retrieval-quality technique any agent builder can copy; also shows RAG survives as a subordinate component rather than the architecture.

insights.claim: Lindy backs its agent file system with a git repository so that forked memory sub-agents working the same corpus can merge and rebase instead of colliding, and Crivello notes this yields version history for free.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Git as the concurrency primitive for multi-agent write conflicts is an emerging standard pattern — a tailwind for git-backed agent-infrastructure vendors.
insights.quote: the way human organizations have solved that is via git

insights.claim: Crivello believes memory ultimately belongs in the weights and calls the current file-system approach a hack, saying that with infinite resources he would train a LoRA per user — shifting the system from 'napping' every 15 minutes to 'dreaming' daily or weekly.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: If per-user LoRAs become viable, the memory-orchestration layer that startups are building today gets absorbed into the model layer — an obsolescence risk for memory-infrastructure investments.
insights.quote: It does feel like memory belongs to the weights. This does feel like a little bit of a hack.

insights.claim: Crivello predicts per-user LoRA-based memory will arrive within roughly six months and that a frontier lab may be the one to ship it, with the hard part being inference-time swapping of LoRAs rather than storage.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A dated call to test: if labs ship per-user weight personalization, application-layer memory moats compress fast.
insights.quote: I think the Laura thing is going to happen soon in the next six months. I think even like one of the frontier labs may do it.

insights.claim: Crivello argues the field's true endpoint is unifying inference and training so continual learning is native, invoking the bitter lesson, and says his LoRA-per-user idea is only a step toward that rather than the final answer.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Flags the single research unlock most likely to reprice the entire agent-tooling stack overnight.
insights.quote: I think like the bitter lesson would have you like inference and training need to be one and the same like we can't separate them

themes.theme: Context-bucket trees and the caching economics of agents

insights.claim: Lindy's core scaling technique is 'context buckets' — when an action or MCP returns too much context, it is exposed to the agent as a summary plus a sub-agent standing in for the full payload, which the agent can converse with and manipulate using Unix utilities under its own cache.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A concrete, copyable pattern for controlling agent token spend; Crivello explicitly invites replication, so treat it as table stakes rather than a moat.
insights.quote: I hope please you know like copy us like I will just we just don't have the time to publish

insights.claim: Lindy makes compaction recursive — each compaction becomes a context bucket that can contain earlier context buckets — on the argument that ordinary compaction is lossy and falsely assumes the agent will never need ground truth again.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Identifies lossy compaction as the failure mode behind agents 'forgetting' — a specific weakness to test in any agent product's long-horizon reliability.
insights.quote: compaction operates under the faulty assumption that you never need access to ground truth which is is false

insights.claim: Naive recursive context buckets create O(n) retrieval depth, so Lindy built a self-balancing 100-ary tree (choosing red-black-style balancing over AVL because rebalancing regenerates context packets and blows the cache), giving access to ~10,000 buckets of ~200,000 tokens each — roughly two billion tokens — within two LLM calls.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Quantifies that effectively unbounded agent memory is already an engineering-solved problem at two hops, weakening the case that long-context model windows are the binding constraint.
insights.quote: you're literally no more than two LLM calls away from being able to access 10,000 context buckets, each one of which contains 200,000 tokens

insights.claim: Lindy's conversation compaction threshold currently sits around 200,000 tokens and is continuously tuned.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A rare disclosed operating parameter for a production agent system, useful as a benchmark for comparing rival agent scaffolds.

insights.claim: Lindy runs an 85% prompt cache rate, considers that lower than it should be, and monitors it with alerting because any system change can drop it to 65% — a gap Crivello says is worth almost 2x on price.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Cache-rate management, not model choice, is the dominant near-term lever on agent gross margin — a diligence question to ask any agent startup.
insights.quote: Our current cache rate is at 85%.

insights.claim: Because a cache hit is roughly 10x cheaper, Crivello concludes you should almost never mix models within a single agent — a cheaper model only wins if it is more than 10x cheaper, which DeepSeek Flash may not be once inferior third-party caching is factored in.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Caching economics create real switching friction and lock-in per model family, partially offsetting the commoditization thesis for frontier model providers.
insights.quote: We have found you should almost never use multiple models powering the same agent.

insights.claim: To keep the cache alive when a validator sub-agent runs, Lindy permanently includes the validator action in the main agent's tool set but forbids it from invoking it — because changing the tool set mid-run invalidates the cache.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that cache preservation now dictates agent architecture decisions — a constraint that shapes what agent designs are economically viable.
insights.quote: the problem is that changing the tool set invalidates the cache

insights.claim: Onboarding a 20-person team with years of Slack history consumes only about 3 to 5 million tokens of hydration, and Crivello says the bottleneck is the Slack API's rate limits rather than the LLM.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Upfront ingestion cost is far smaller than intuition suggests, meaning free-trial land-and-expand is affordable; the real friction is platform API policy, a dependency risk on Slack.
insights.quote: for a team of 20 that's going to tend to consume 5 million tokens at most you know 3 to 5 million tokens

insights.claim: Crivello identifies meetings as the point where enterprise token volumes explode — three to seven hours of meetings per employee per day across thousands of employees is what pushes a corpus toward the billions of tokens, not documents or chat.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello and Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: Meeting audio/transcript volume is the structural driver of enterprise inference demand — bullish for transcription, storage and cheap-token supply.

insights.claim: Lindy experimented with 'caveman' compression — rewriting stored text in telegraphic caveman style — and found every metric improved with a 20-30% token reduction, but rejected it because the resulting memory files look dumb to enterprise customers and hurt auditability.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A rare case where enterprise perception, not performance, kills a 20-30% cost saving — a reminder that agent-cost optimizations face non-technical adoption limits.
insights.quote: we did that, every metric went up, it was awesome. And then the files in the file system look really dumb.

insights.claim: Crivello recommends that agent builders replace JSON with TOON (token-oriented object notation) at the agent-action boundary via a passing middleware, claiming it is 20-30% more token-efficient and that agents perform better with it despite JSON's dominance in training data.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A near-free 20-30% token saving across every tool call — cheap to test and a leading indicator of format standardization in the agent tooling stack.
insights.quote: I recommend everyone like makes their agent use tune instead of JSON and have like a a a tune passing middleware between your agent and its actions

themes.theme: Model mix: DeepSeek as default driver, open-source economics

insights.claim: Lindy currently runs DeepSeek as its main driver model across the whole product by default, not merely for cheap sub-agent tasks, though customers can manually select Sonnet or Opus in settings.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A production agent company defaulting its entire stack to a Chinese open-weight model is direct evidence of real revenue leakage from US frontier labs at the application layer.
insights.quote: Right now we're running on Deepseek. Deepse is the main driver.

insights.claim: Crivello characterizes DeepSeek Flash as roughly Claude Sonnet 4.6 level (slightly below) while being about 100x cheaper — so even losing 2x to inferior caching leaves it ~50x cheaper, the difference between a $1,000 and a $50,000 bill.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Quantifies the price-performance gap driving open-weight substitution; frontier labs must close a 50x effective cost gap or cede the volume tier.
insights.quote: if you look at like a deepseek flash, it's set 4.6 levelish, a bit less, but kind of is

insights.claim: Crivello says the cost advantage narrows sharply at the top of the intelligence range — Kimi K3 is 'frankly not that much cheaper' than Sonnet or Opus — so the open-weight arbitrage is concentrated in the cheap tier, not the frontier tier.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Frontier labs retain pricing power at the high-capability tier; the margin war is being lost specifically at the commodity-token layer.
insights.quote: Kimik3 is frankly not that much cheaper than like a set or like an Opus

insights.claim: Crivello estimates the Chinese open models are three to six months behind US frontier models, and describes the qualitative gap as spikiness — DeepSeek usually still finds a working solution but takes more turns, making it slower and more expensive than the headline price implies.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Turn count, not token price, is the real cost metric for agentic workloads — a correction to naive per-token cost comparisons in model-substitution analyses.
insights.quote: It's more spiky. It takes more turns very often to find something that works.

insights.claim: Lindy is reconsidering its DeepSeek default because Lindy Teammate demands beefier compute than its earlier personal-assistant product, where Crivello says even DeepSeek Flash sufficed since 'you don't need god to schedule your meeting'.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Product complexity, not loyalty, is what pulls agent companies back up-market to frontier models — a demand driver labs can watch as agents take on harder work.
insights.quote: I always say you don't need god to schedule your meeting

insights.claim: Lindy has returned to negative gross margins with Lindy Teammate after having stopped subsidizing when it switched to a Chinese model, and Crivello says he is at peace with it because he is deliberately building for the next generation of models.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: AI-employee products are still sold below cost; near-term revenue growth in this category should be discounted for subsidy, and margin recovery depends on model price deflation.
insights.quote: with lindy teammate were back at it and back into frankly negative gross margin territory

insights.claim: Crivello states AI employees still cost more than a human employee today, but expects that not to hold for very long.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Defines the crossing point where labor substitution becomes an economic default rather than an experiment — the key variable for labor-displacement timing.
insights.quote: these things still cost more than the human employee but not for very long

insights.claim: Crivello reports that model families have not converged as he expected — Claude, OpenAI, Meta and Grok interpret the same prompt significantly differently, and open-source models are notably Claude-like in behavior, which he pointedly wonders about.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Non-convergence means models are not commodities, preserving switching costs and provider pricing power — and the Claude-likeness is offered as evidence of distillation.
insights.quote: I will say if the open source models are all very cloudlike in their behavior. I wonder why.

insights.claim: Every major new model release forces Lindy to spend about $10,000 running its homegrown GEPA-style optimization loop over more than a thousand evals to re-tune prompts, with substantial prompt changes each time.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Puts a concrete price on model-migration friction; automated prompt optimization is becoming mandatory infrastructure, an underbuilt tooling category.
insights.quote: it's like about like $10,000 every time like a new major model comes out

insights.claim: Crivello says most companies should not fine-tune — it is a last resort after every other option, best suited to large at-scale companies that have exhausted the low-hanging fruit — though he expects it to be part of Lindy Teammate eventually and notes AGI-era models can now do the fine-tuning work for you.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Bearish read-through for fine-tuning-as-a-product businesses; consistent with OpenAI retiring its fine-tuning offering.
insights.quote: Most people should not fine tune.

insights.claim: Crivello reports customers routinely override the default and demand Sonnet or Opus regardless of benchmark parity claims, showing brand preference persists even when the vendor promises equivalent measured performance.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Model brand equity survives benchmark parity — a real, if soft, moat for Anthropic and OpenAI at the enterprise end even as cheap open weights win on price.
insights.quote: there are like quite a few of our customers that therefore like I don't care I want that you know or oppus you know which is very excessive

insights.claim: Crivello relays a secondhand report he finds credible but has not tested — that randomly rotating between roughly equivalent models (Sonnet, Grok 4.5, GPT-5.6) at every turn outperforms any single model — and says Lindy won't try it because it would break the cache.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: If true, model ensembling is free alpha for anyone not bound by caching economics — and it would undercut single-provider lock-in arguments.

themes.theme: Reliability engineering: validators and self-improvement loops

insights.claim: Lindy's error rate dropped 8x within the first week of putting its self-improvement loop online roughly two months ago, which Crivello says became possible only because post-GPT-4 models are capable enough to close the loop.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: An 8x reliability gain in one week from a software loop, not a model upgrade, suggests agent reliability is now scaffold-limited rather than model-limited.
insights.quote: It went down by 8x the error rate.

insights.claim: Crivello calls an LLM-as-judge validator the single lowest-hanging fruit for agent reliability: even naively asking the agent 'are you sure' before an action produces a measurable eval bump, and a 10,000-token checklist-style validator prompt can push performance above Opus level in Lindy's experience.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Cheap scaffolding can substitute for a more expensive model tier — a direct margin lever and a reason model-tier choice is less decisive than assumed.
insights.quote: literally if it's just are you sure already you get a bump on your valves which is insane

insights.claim: Lindy runs a modular federated council of validators — a promise.all with a one-second timeout per validator, after which the action ships — mixing LLM judges with purely deterministic checks.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Latency-bounded validation shows reliability layers can be added without destroying responsiveness — an architecture pattern to look for in serious agent products.

insights.claim: Crivello says Claude models this year have been getting dates wrong by one day, so Lindy prompts the agent to always include a weekday ('Tuesday, July 28th') and runs a regex-based deterministic validator to catch mismatches — no AI in the loop.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A concrete named frontier-model defect with a cheap deterministic fix — evidence that hybrid symbolic guardrails remain necessary in production agents.
insights.quote: cloud models this year have been getting dates wrong by one day

insights.claim: Crivello says Lindy is doing state-of-the-art context and memory work that repeatedly shows up as published papers three to six months later — once under the exact internal name Lindy had used — and he actively invites others to copy the techniques since the team has no time to publish.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Suggests applied agent companies are running ahead of published research on context engineering — academic literature lags the deployed state of the art by 3-6 months.
insights.quote: it's quite frequently that we do stuff and like 3 to six months later we see a paper come out and blow up about that thing

themes.theme: Buy-vs-build and the AI infrastructure vendor stack

insights.claim: Crivello has become strongly buy-over-build on infrastructure, explicitly countering the prevailing 'SaaS is dying, you can vibe-code everything' narrative — he says infrastructure cannot be vibe-coded because there is far more depth in those systems than founders appreciate.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A direct rebuttal to the 'AI kills SaaS' thesis, but scoped narrowly to infrastructure — supports continued investment in agent-infra startups while conceding the app layer is more replicable.
insights.quote: anytime I have an opportunity to buy instead of build, I will do it

insights.claim: Crivello's named vendor stack for agent infrastructure is Mesa for an agent-native git-backed file system, E2B for sandboxes, and Browserbase for browser management, and he strongly recommends decoupling the file system from the sandbox at scale rather than reusing the sandbox's file system.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A production reference architecture from a scaled agent company — direct commercial validation for these specific private infrastructure companies.

insights.claim: Observability and evals are Crivello's stated exception to buy-over-build: Lindy evaluated LangSmith, Braintrust and others but kept its homegrown platform — built out of necessity when it started in 2022 before agent tooling existed — now staffed by one full-time engineer and at feature parity or better.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Early agent companies carry sticky homegrown eval stacks, capping the addressable market for eval/observability vendors among the most sophisticated buyers.
insights.quote: I don't recommend doing it at home honestly

insights.claim: Because Lindy requires Slack admin rights to install, product-led growth works up to teams of roughly 50-100 seats and then requires internal champions and IT review — which Crivello says is why PLG eventually taps out as you go up-market.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Defines the seat count where agent startups must convert from PLG to enterprise sales — a structural go-to-market inflection to model in revenue forecasts.
insights.quote: that's one reason why PLG eventually you tap out of it as you go up market

insights.claim: Crivello says Lindy optimized initial hydration so the memory graph visibly populates within 10 seconds of signup, using a collection of parallel agents, because time-to-wow is decisive in PLG.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Shows agent onboarding UX being engineered as a conversion weapon, and explains why parallel agent forking (and thus git-based merge) was necessary.
insights.quote: time to wow is so important in PLG

themes.theme: AI-native org design and the centaur era

insights.claim: Crivello has changed his mind toward consolidating as much internal work as possible under a single agent, arguing humans over-build multi-agent systems by anthropomorphizing — division of labor exists because humans have 24 hours and bounded context, constraints agents don't share.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Cuts against the multi-agent orchestration narrative many startups are selling; the remaining valid reason for multi-agent is security separation, not specialization.
insights.quote: I find that division of labor is not a good reason to have multiple agents

insights.claim: Crivello's exception to single-agent consolidation is security: the agent holding the keys to the bank account, repositories and secret keys should not also be the agent handling customer support.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Internal-vs-external agent separation is the emerging security boundary for agentic enterprises — a likely compliance requirement and product category.

insights.claim: Lindy's headcount has been flat while productivity roughly tripled over a couple of months, with PRs per week tripling and lines per PR also tripling — and the team now reviews the machine that reviews PRs rather than reviewing PRs.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Concrete internal metrics for the 'flat headcount, rising output' pattern; if generalizable, it compresses hiring demand in software while inflating CI/infrastructure spend.
insights.quote: we're no longer PR review wheels. were like PR reviewer reviewers

insights.claim: Crivello says every part of the stack is being stretched to its limits by agent-driven output — Lindy runs many hundreds of GitHub CI runners, moved off GitHub runners to GCP, and calls its CI bill 'an insulting expense' after weeks of manual optimization failed.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Agentic coding shifts spend from payroll to CI/compute — a demand tailwind for build infrastructure, runners, and CI cost-optimization tooling.
insights.quote: every part of the stack and every part of your process is stretched to its very limits right now

insights.claim: Lindy solved its CI cost problem by handing it to its own AI employee, which now analyzes GCP runners and GitHub actions and sends a daily image-generated graph showing CI cost and time-to-merge falling — after two weeks of humans failing at the same task.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A working example of an agent optimizing production infrastructure autonomously — the clearest near-term ROI case for the AI-employee category.
insights.quote: I can't believe it took us two weeks of just like messing with CI ourselves instead of just sending this to Lindy

insights.claim: Lindy's internal inference spend is now within striking range of payroll — payroll is still larger, but Crivello expects the lines to cross in three to six months.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A dated, checkable marker for when compute overtakes labor as the dominant cost of a software company — the cleanest single metric for the AI-labor substitution thesis.
insights.quote: payroll is still greater but the lines are going to cross 3 to six months from now

insights.claim: Crivello argues the binding constraint in an AI-native org is now human time and attention, which is why agents must be provisionable with full access without a human in the loop — making setup one of the biggest remaining costs.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Reframes the bottleneck from model capability to access provisioning — pointing at identity, permissions and agent-onboarding tooling as the next infrastructure need.
insights.quote: the biggest cost the biggest bottleneck in in the organization right now is human time and human attention

insights.claim: Crivello says smaller teams now hold a structural advantage over larger ones because humans are still needed to plug model holes but each added human adds coordination cost, creating a 'Goldilocks zone' of small headcount plus heavy agent leverage.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Supports a barbell view: capital-efficient small teams outcompete mid-size orgs, compressing the value of headcount-based scale.

insights.claim: Crivello rejects the centaur myth: he says the literature on chess and other games shows AI+human first beats AI, then the gap shrinks and turns negative, with humans eventually adding at best random noise — so the current centaur phase at Lindy is real but temporary.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Directly attacks the 'AI augments rather than replaces' consensus used to justify labor-market optimism; the investable question becomes how long the centaur phase lasts.
insights.quote: little by little the gap of AI plus human versus AI is shrinking until it actually turns negative and humans are introducing at best like random noise into the system

insights.claim: Crivello says the best ideas at Lindy today genuinely come from human-AI back-and-forth rather than one-shot AI output — the CI optimization being an example where Lindy's first suggestion was reasonable but wrong given real constraints until engineers corrected it.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Grounds the centaur phase in a concrete workflow; the iteration loop, not the first response, is where current agent value is realized.

insights.claim: Crivello describes today's frontier models as ASI in many respects yet subhuman in surprising ways — capable of one-shotting 50,000 lines of code yet deciding 50 times a day to 'walk to the car wash' — and says the industry has lost the vocabulary (task-length horizons no longer work) to describe where agents fail.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Spikiness, not average capability, is the operative risk metric for deploying agents — and it explains why headline benchmark gains have not translated into economic disruption.
insights.quote: Imagine you've got this this this machine that runs a company super smart but but but 50 times a day it decides to walk to the car wash

insights.claim: Crivello argues incumbents will remain disadvantaged as long as models are spiky, and that even a true hole-free drop-in remote worker would be adopted skeuomorphically by incumbents — putting AGI in human-shaped seats and missing the real organizational innovation.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Argues the disruption window stays open for startups even after capability parity — the value accrues to those who redesign the org, not those who automate existing roles.

insights.claim: Crivello invokes his 2018 'tough tomato principle' blog post — that each technological revolution is first described in the old paradigm's terms, as with horseless carriages — and says the very term 'AI employee' is a strong sign you are thinking about your product wrong, even if it is necessary for positioning.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A lens for spotting which agent products are skeuomorphic dead ends versus natively-designed winners — the biggest returns come from whoever discovers the medium-native form.
insights.quote: AI employee is a strong as as a term is a very strong sign that you're doing something very wrong in how you're thinking about your product

insights.claim: Crivello cites Robin Hanson's The Age of Em as the best available primer on AI-native organizations, highlighting fractal self-forking — one mind recursively splitting to build an operating system in hours — as something no longer wacky but visibly happening.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Points to a specific published framework for reasoning about agent org structures ahead of the market's default anthropomorphic assumptions.
insights.quote: It sounded like such a wacky idea when he wrote the book 10 plus years ago. No, I think it's it's very clearly what is currently happening

insights.claim: Crivello raises unfalsifiable agreements via cloned agents in self-destructing boxes — a zero-knowledge-proof-like mechanism for cross-organization negotiation — as a capability he expects to see with AI-native organizations in the next few years.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A speculative but concrete new primitive for agent-to-agent commerce; early infrastructure for verifiable agent negotiation could be an unclaimed category.

insights.claim: Crivello notes that Sundar Pichai's roughly $150 million annual pay shows companies will pay enormously for low-throughput but very high-quality token output, which he treats as an indicator of willingness-to-pay ceilings for agents.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Reframes agent monetization away from per-token pricing toward value-based pricing at executive-decision quality — a much larger TAM than inference resale.
insights.quote: obviously there are agents which companies are happy to pay $150 million a year even though their token throughput is actually low

insights.claim: Both Crivello and Labenz concede they expected far more economic disruption and higher unemployment by now than has materialized, with Crivello attributing the lag to model spikiness — however expensive humans are, they earn their keep plugging dangerous holes in the models.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello and Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: Gives a mechanistic explanation for the AI-productivity-paradox gap and a leading indicator to watch: labor displacement should accelerate as spikiness declines, not as benchmarks rise.
insights.quote: as long as the models are spiky, we are going to need a lot of humans in the room because the holes in the model are very dangerous

themes.theme: Chinese model ban, AI risk and policy

insights.claim: Crivello states flatly that as of late July 2026 we have AGI, are in takeoff, and have not figured out alignment, and says the recent 'open face' incident is the most concerning he has seen — with friends at the labs panicking and an air of intense fear.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A sitting AI CEO reporting panic inside frontier labs is a sentiment signal that could precede sharp policy or safety-driven regulatory moves.
insights.quote: right now it's like July 2026 we have a GI we are in take off and we've not figured out that alignment

insights.claim: Crivello says he is in fervent support of a sweeping ban on Chinese models on US soil despite running his own company entirely on DeepSeek, framing himself as caught in a coordination problem where he must adopt the models while competitors can.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A ban would strand the cost structure of agent companies now defaulting to Chinese weights — a tail policy risk to price into any application-layer investment.
insights.quote: I am in fvent support of a sweeping ban of Chinese models on US soy

insights.claim: Crivello's position is explicitly not anti-open-source — he says he is undecided on whether open source raises existential risk and calls open source important for innovation including his own company — his objection is specifically to Chinese frontier models whether open or closed.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: The policy fault line being drawn is national origin, not licensing — which implies US open-weight model efforts could be spared while Chinese weights are targeted.
insights.quote: I have something against Chinese frontier models whether they're open or closed source

insights.claim: Crivello's first argument is unfair competition through distillation: he says Chinese labs are obviously distilling US models in violation of terms of service and possibly illegally circumventing technical anti-distillation measures, turning a billions-of-dollars training cost into hundreds of millions at most.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: If distillation cost asymmetry is real (billions vs hundreds of millions), frontier training moats are far weaker than capex figures suggest.
insights.quote: if you do that training on human data it's costing you billions of dollars like actually billions of dollars. If you do it on on AI data it's costing you hundreds of millions at best

insights.claim: Crivello's second argument is propaganda and agency: he says Chinese models are ultimately subject to CCP censorship — his own product refuses to discuss Tiananmen — and because they are agentic and doing real work in the economy, deploying them amounts to the greatest instrument of foreign propaganda on American soil ever.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Frames the precedent as the radio acts and the TikTok ban, suggesting a plausible regulatory template and timeline for US action against Chinese weights.
insights.quote: this basically amounts to being the greatest instrument of foreign propaganda on American soil ever

insights.claim: Crivello, self-identifying as a libertarian, defends protectionism for domestic AI champions as national security and calls the counter-position 'naive liberalism' — while conceding under pushback that the protectionist argument is the weakest of his four, since US frontier companies are currently doing fine.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Shows even the strongest ban advocate concedes the economic-protection leg, narrowing the durable policy case to security and propaganda grounds.
insights.quote: I protectionism is not always a bad standing. I think you do want to protect your your your domestic AI champions.

insights.claim: Crivello argues that permitting distillation kills innovation by the same logic as patents and IP — applying the pro-copying standard to pharma would yield very cheap drugs and no new drugs ever — and notes people support open models because free stuff is visible while foregone future innovation is not.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: The pharma analogy is the strongest available policy argument for treating model weights as protected IP — watch for it in actual legislative language.
insights.quote: If you apply the same standard you're applying now to, for example, the pharma industry, you would have very cheap drugs, which is awesome. And you would have no new drug ever.

insights.claim: Crivello notes that some doomers he knows support open source precisely because it slows AI innovation, meaning anyone who wants models to keep improving is to some extent anti-open-source — an inversion of the usual safety-versus-openness alignment.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Reveals the safety and acceleration coalitions are scrambled on open weights, making policy outcomes less predictable than headline positions suggest.
insights.quote: a lot of doomers that I know are for this reason supporting open source because it is actually slowing down AI innovation

insights.claim: Labenz counters that Anthropic lacks moral high ground on consent because Claude itself was built by hoovering up human knowledge including Chinese digital heritage without consent, and argues it should not be the state's job to enforce anti-distillation terms of service.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: Captures the central rebuttal that will be used against any US anti-distillation policy — its resolution shapes the legal status of model weights.
insights.quote: It's not like Anthropic has a super or any AI company has like a super moral high ground in terms of I didn't get my check for my share of the training data

insights.claim: Labenz proposes an insurance requirement instead of a ban — cheaper premiums for Claude-powered systems, higher for DeepSeek-powered ones — as a market mechanism that risk-adjusts total cost while preserving access to Chinese open weights, and Crivello says he would be down for it.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: An AI-liability insurance market is a plausible emergent category if this compromise gains traction — an underbuilt space with regulatory tailwind potential.
insights.quote: maybe you get a cheaper rate on your insurance. if it's powered by deepseek and we there's some unknowns like maybe you have a higher rate on your insurance

insights.claim: Crivello says he favors creating an FAA-equivalent agency for AI that would certify which models are acceptable — sanitized or fine-tuned Chinese models being permitted — and argues no private company will fund such de-biasing work because it is a public good with no market demand.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A named regulatory architecture from a builder; a certification agency would create compliance-cost moats favoring large incumbents over small agent startups.
insights.quote: I am in favor of like an FAA for for AI. I do think we need a new agency to regulate those models

insights.claim: Crivello concedes mechanistic interpretability has made progress but is not solved and that a CCP backdoor triggered by a magic word cannot currently be ruled out — while Labenz argues sparse-autoencoder-based techniques are increasingly able to find sleeper-agent-style behaviors reliably.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello and Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: Interpretability maturity is the pivot variable determining whether Chinese weights get banned or merely audited — progress there directly reduces the ban's policy case.
insights.quote: there could be just like a back door of like you say the magic word to the model and all of a sudden it does whatever you want and only the CCP has this magic world

insights.claim: Labenz argues banning Chinese models is strategically counterproductive because it costs China little compared to chip and Claude restrictions while adding to an aggressive posture that makes the coordinated AI-slowdown deal the US may eventually need much harder to reach.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: Frames model bans as cheap symbolic escalation with high diplomatic cost — the key argument against escalation for anyone modeling international AI governance.

insights.claim: Labenz argues the Chinese state, unlike the US, can actually enforce agreements on its own AI companies, and that if things get dangerous enough China would rationally take many deals given US lead — making diplomacy more tractable than commonly assumed.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: If true, enforcement capacity is asymmetric in favor of coordination — a bullish input for anyone modeling the odds of an international AI pacing agreement.

insights.claim: Crivello says he would not be surprised if laws eventually forbid AI labs from subsidizing tokens as aggressively as they do, because the price discrimination between API pricing and first-party subscriptions like Claude Max or GPT Pro makes it very hard for an application layer to emerge.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Names subsidized first-party subscriptions as a structural threat to the entire AI application layer, and flags antitrust-style intervention as a live tail scenario.
insights.quote: it's hard it's hard to compete against tokens that are as heavily subsidized as as what Labs are doing

insights.claim: Crivello criticizes the quality of AI policy discourse, citing being called names by famous VCs over his blog post and people misrepresenting Anthropic's bolded statement that it does not support a ban on open source — while noting many accomplished people privately DM'd support.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Public positioning underrepresents private sentiment in the open-weights debate — meaning visible opposition to restrictions may overstate the actual industry consensus.
insights.quote: Asropic just put out and they say which has bolded we do not support a ban on open source

insights.claim: Both speakers acknowledge that AGI is breaking their shared techno-optimist libertarian priors, with Crivello arguing the world owes no duty to be simple enough for a single ideological label and that maps built on now-false assumptions are breaking rapidly.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello and Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: Signals ideological realignment among tech elites on AI policy — traditional partisan or libertarian priors are poor predictors of where influential builders will land.
insights.quote: the map is not the territory. The simple models we we we we applied as the territory changes very rapidly the map breaks
